title: Proof by induction
examples: When do I need to use induction for a proof?
What is the hardest part of the inductive step?
How do I write the final conclusion clearly?

explain.say: Today we learn proof by induction. This method proves statements about all natural numbers. It has three main parts you must follow.
First we check the base case. This means we prove the statement is true for the smallest number, usually one. You must always start here.

items: Prove statement is true for n=1

explain.say: Next we assume the statement is true for some number n. This is the inductive hypothesis. We then prove it must also be true for n plus one.
Finally we state the conclusion clearly. We say that because the first case works and the step works, it is true for all numbers.

Let us prove the sum of the first n integers. The formula is n squared plus n divided by two. For n equals one, the sum is one. The formula gives one squared plus one divided by two, which is one point five. Wait, the sum is just one. So the formula is wrong for n=1. Let us use the sum of the first n odd numbers. The formula is n squared. For n equals one, the sum is one. The formula gives one squ

draw.text: Sum of first n odd numbers: 1^2 + ... + (2n-1)^2 = n^2

faq.q: What if the formula is not for a sum?
faq.a: Induction can prove statements about sequences too. You just need to adapt the hypothesis and the step accordingly. You might need to look at the relationship between terms.
asks: Can I use induction for something else?
Does it only work for sums?

faq.q: If the base case fails, what does that mean?
faq.a: If the base case fails, the entire statement is false. You cannot proceed to the inductive step because the foundation is not proven true.
asks: Must the base case always work?
If n=1 fails, is the proof over?

faq.q: What exactly do I assume in the inductive hypothesis?
faq.a: You assume that the statement is true for an arbitrary natural number n. You write this assumption down clearly before starting the algebra.
asks: How do I write the assumption part?

faq.q: Is the conclusion just a summary sentence?
faq.a: Yes, the conclusion formally states that the statement holds for all natural numbers greater than or equal to the base case. It closes the proof.
asks: Do I need to write anything after the proof?
What should the final sentence say?

faq.q: Can I use induction if the statement is only true for even numbers?
faq.a: Induction is best for statements true for all integers from a starting point. If it only works for even numbers, you might need to prove it separately for the even sequence.
asks: What if the set is not all natural numbers?

facts: Induction proves statements for all natural numbers starting from a base case.
The base case proves the statement is true for the smallest number, usually one.
The inductive step shows that if it is true for n, it must be true for n plus one.
The conclusion summarizes that the statement is true for all numbers in the set.

quiz.say: If you are proving a formula for the sum of the first n integers, what must you check first?

options.show: Show it works for n equals two.
options.say: Show it works for n equals two.

options.show: Assume it works for n equals two.
options.say: Assume it works for n equals two.

options.show: The formula must hold true when n equals one.
options.say: The formula must hold true when n equals one.

quiz.why: The base case ensures the formula is correct for the smallest value in the set.

wrong.0: This is checking a second case, but you must always start with the very first case.
wrong.1: You must prove the base case first, not just assume it for a higher number.
wrong.2: The inductive step relies on the base case being true first.

quiz.say: In the inductive step, what do you assume is true?

options.show: You assume the statement is true for an arbitrary number n.
options.say: You assume the statement is true for an arbitrary number n.

options.show: Assume the statement is true for n minus one.
options.say: Assume the statement is true for n minus one.

options.show: Assume the statement is true for n plus one.
options.say: Assume the statement is true for n plus one.

options.show: Assume the statement is true for n equals one.
options.say: Assume the statement is true for n equals one.

quiz.why: This assumption allows you to manipulate the equation for n to derive the equation for n plus one.

wrong.1: You must assume it is true for n to prove it for n plus one.
wrong.2: If you assume it for n plus one, you have already proven what you needed to prove.
wrong.3: That is the base case, which is a specific number, not a general assumption.

quiz.say: What is the purpose of the final conclusion in an induction proof?

options.show: It formally states the statement is true for all natural numbers from the base c
options.say: It formally states the statement is true for all natural numbers from the base c

options.show: It means you do not need to write any more math.
options.say: It means you do not need to write any more math.

options.show: It only proves it works for n equals one.
options.say: It only proves it works for n equals one.

options.show: It is just a summary of the steps taken.
options.say: It is just a summary of the steps taken.

quiz.why: This sentence wraps up the logic, confirming the pattern continues forever.

wrong.1: While you do not write more math, the conclusion itself is a formal mathematical statement.
wrong.2: The conclusion covers all numbers, not just the starting point.
wrong.3: It is more than a summary; it is a definitive claim of universal truth.
